sketch: Smallest instance: factor N=15 with base a=2 (order r=4). Registers: t=4 counting qubits (ordered little-endian, integer x=sum x_k 2^k) and 4 work qubits holding y mod 15, initialized to |0>^t|0001>. Ideal algorithm: (1) Hadamard on all counting qubits; (2) controlled modular multiplications |x>|y> -> |x>|a^x y mod N>, compiled as controlled U^(2^k) with U|y>=|a y mod N>; (3) inverse QFT on the counting register, built from H and controlled-phase gates CP(pi/2^m); (4) decoding, which is outside the unitary and would measure the counting register to get x, take the continued fraction of x/2^t to get r, then compute gcd(a^(r/2)+-1, N). Gate-imperfection model (the abstract names three categories without defining them, so these definitions are my assumptions). Systematic error: every controlled-phase angle theta is replaced by theta(1+eps) or theta+delta with a fixed eps/delta, applied identically at every occurrence. Random error: each phase gate gets an independent offset delta_j drawn from a zero-mean distribution of width sigma, with several seeds averaged. Combined error: a fixed offset plus an independent random offset. The circuit builder inserts the perturbed phase gates in the QFT, and optionally small Rz rotations after the modular-arithmetic gates, using explicit numeric error values. The success probability is then computed as the probability mass on counting outcomes x whose x/2^t is within rounding of s/r, and compared with the ideal value. The claimed behaviour is that fixed offsets shift the peak coherently and are largely tolerated, while random offsets add up as incoherent noise whose damage grows with the number of gates and thus with log N. A threshold sigma_c(N) can be defined as the largest sigma for which the averaged success probability stays above a chosen cutoff, such as half the ideal value. This sketch does not derive the paper's analytic threshold formula.
